tldr: We propose RPG, a framework that dramatically boosts robot manipulation success without updating any model weights, by autonomously evolving shared skill code and system prompts through practice in simulation.
hero_caption: Overall workflow of the RPG framework. It reconstructs practice tasks from an offline dataset (Reconstruct), diagnoses failures by comparing execution videos between a privileged agent with ground-truth simulator state and a real-compatible runtime agent, and autonomously refines and updates a shared skill library (Practice).
overview:
When getting robots to perform diverse tasks, manually rebuilding skills for each task, tuning reward functions, and integrating perception with control is exhausting work. Program-generation approaches like Code-as-Policy run fast and reliably, but struggle with flexible perceptual judgments. Conversely, Agent-as-Policy approaches that keep an MLLM (multimodal large language model) in the loop suffer from high inference latency.

To address this, the authors asked: "What if we autonomously improve shared skill code and system prompts instead of fine-tuning model weights?" and developed RPG (Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real). First, it reconstructs practice tasks in a simulation environment from an offline dataset. Then, it runs both a normal agent operating solely on real-compatible observations and a privileged agent with full ground-truth simulator state. By comparing and diagnosing execution outcomes and failure videos from both, an LLM agent automatically adds missing skills, fixes bugs, and refines the system prompt.

Evaluated on held-out initializations across 22 manipulation tasks in simulation, task success surged from 28.6% before practice to 95.0% after 15 autonomous practice rounds, substantially outperforming recent baselines like GPT-6 Astra Pro (60.0%). Furthermore, after applying only a common hardware calibration procedure, the improved system was deployed directly to a physical bimanual robot with no additional training or manual tuning, achieving a 100% success rate across all 30 trials on three evaluated tasks.
contributions: Proposed RPG, a framework that elevates robot execution performance purely through autonomous updates to a shared code library and prompt, without modifying any model weights.
Developed a diagnosis mechanism that identifies failure causes by comparing execution trajectories and videos between a Privileged Agent with ground-truth simulator state and a normal agent.
Introduced a verification gate using cross-task testing and merged re-testing to prevent individual skill fixes and prompt updates from causing regressions on other tasks.
Deployed the frozen system practiced in simulation zero-shot to a physical bimanual robot, achieving 100% success across all 30 trials over 3 tasks (10 trials each).

sections.heading: Evolving Code Without Changing Model Weights: A New Paradigm
sections.summary: To combine the fast execution of programs with the flexible reasoning of MLLMs in robot control, we propose the self-improving RPG framework. Through practice in simulation, it autonomously polishes a shared skill library and prompt, enabling real-world deployment.
sections.details:
Advances in multimodal LLMs have dramatically improved capabilities for visual scene understanding, reasoning, and code generation. However, when applied to robot control, there is an inherent trade-off between the "Code-as-Policy" approach (generating and executing code) and the "Agent-as-Policy" approach (keeping an LLM continuously in the control loop). The former handles repetitive motions rapidly, but writing explicit logic for visual judgments like "is the object securely grasped?" is difficult. The latter offers flexible decision-making, but frequent model invocations make execution sluggish.

An ideal system is hybrid: offloading repetitive, deterministic execution to reusable code while reserving MLLM reasoning strictly for moments that require visual and semantic judgment.

In this work, we propose RPG (Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real), a framework that progressively evolves a shared skill library and system prompt through autonomous practice in simulation without updating any model weights (parameters). By reconstructing practice tasks from offline data and automatically revising code through detailed execution diagnoses, RPG successfully raised simulation task success from 28.6% to 95.0%.

sections.heading: How It Differs: Privileged Diagnosis and Cross-Task Code Verification
sections.summary: We review prior work on robot program generation, skill accumulation, and offline data utilization. RPG is unique in that it avoids neural network training, using privileged failure diagnosis and regression-tested code revisions instead.
sections.details:
### II-A Improvements in Robot Programs and Skills
Extensive research has explored using LLMs to generate executable robot code (Code as Policies, ProgPrompt, CaP-X, etc.) and leveraging execution feedback to repair plans (Inner Monologue, REFLECT, etc.). Methods that accumulate reusable skills in a library through trial and error (Voyager, LRLL, ASPIRE, RATs, etc.) have also been proposed. RPG fundamentally differs from these by diagnosing failures through the gap between a "privileged agent with ground-truth simulator state" and a "normal agent," updating both the shared skill code and the system prompt, and strictly testing and merging changes across a fixed task suite to prevent regressions on other tasks.

### II-B Offline Data and Simulation Practice
Substantial work also focuses on learning code or policies from demonstration videos and trajectories (Demo2Code, Uni-Skill, etc.) or generating data and tasks in simulation (MimicGen, GenSim, Eureka, etc.). RPG extracts manipulation capability targets from an offline dataset (here, the ABC dataset containing 193 tasks) to construct practice simulation environments. However, instead of mimicking trajectories directly or training a neural network, RPG uniquely utilizes simulation to debug and improve the execution code itself.

sections.heading: The Three Stages of RPG: Reconstruct, Practice, and Go Real
sections.summary: The system consists of six specialized agents. It builds tasks from offline data (Reconstruct), refines and tests skills using privileged state and video diagnosis (Practice), and deploys the frozen system to real hardware after calibration (Go Real).
sections.details:
### III-A Agent-as-Policy Setup and Initialization
RPG coordinates six specialized agents (Constructor, Runtime Agent, Privileged Agent, Video Analyzer, Implementor, Merger) that divide the work of environment building and code revision. The execution system $S_r = (\mathcal{L}_r, \rho_r)$ comprises a shared skill library $\mathcal{L}_r$ and a system prompt $\rho_r$, with model weights remaining frozen. The initial library $\mathcal{L}_0$ contains 15 skills in total: 9 low-level tools and 6 basic manipulation skills generated from demonstrations (pick, place, push, etc.).

### III-B Reconstruct: Building and Freezing Practice Tasks
The Constructor selects tasks covering diverse capabilities from the dataset and builds practice tasks in a MuJoCo environment. It does not need to reproduce the original scene completely, but captures the core manipulation (e.g., turning sunglasses cleanup into a "close an open case" task). Success evaluation functions $e_i(\tau)$ are also generated automatically and frozen after human pre-verification.

### III-C Practice: System Improvement from Execution Feedback
In each practice round, both the normal agent (Runtime Agent) and the privileged agent (Privileged Agent), which also receives the full internal simulator state $S_t$ (exact object poses, velocities, etc.), execute tasks from the same initial conditions. When a failure occurs, the Video Analyzer compares both agents' trajectories and videos against reference dataset videos, pinpoints where the behavior broke down, and issues concrete revision proposals. The Implementor then writes new skill code or prompt revisions based on this feedback.

### III-D Verification and Integration of System Revisions
To prevent code changes aimed at fixing one task from breaking another ("regression"), candidate revisions $\widetilde{S}$ are tested across all tasks (22 tasks $\times$ 5 seeds each). Only candidates that satisfy an improvement in average success rate $\Delta\widehat{J} > 0$ with no individual task degrading by more than 1/5 (20 percentage points) are merged by the Merger. After merging, the code must pass the full-task suite evaluation once more before being officially incorporated into the library.

### III-E Go Real: Hardware Adaptation and Freezing
The finalized system is deployed to physical hardware after minimal coordinate calibration, such as gripper offset tuning. On the real robot, neither the privileged agent nor the diagnosis mechanism is used; inference runs entirely with the frozen system code and prompt.

sections.heading: Dramatic Gains: 95% in Simulation and 30/30 Perfect Real-Robot Trials
sections.summary: Across 22 simulation tasks, 15 practice rounds boosted success from 28.6% to 95.0%, greatly outperforming prior methods and GPT-6 Astra Pro. Ablations confirmed the critical role of privileged diagnosis, and real-world trials achieved 100% across all 30 attempts over 3 tasks.
sections.details:
### IV-A Evaluation Setup and Protocol
Evaluation was conducted using a bimanual 6-DoF robot (YAM) on 22 tasks derived from ABC and CaP-X. Disturbances such as object pose shifts, camera pose variations, and depth noise were injected. Testing used a held-out set of 10 seeds (220 episodes total) completely separated from the 5 seeds used during improvement.

### IV-B Q1: How Much Does Practice Improve Performance?
RPG (runtime model: Gemini 3.8 Flash, offline revision: Fable 5.1) achieved an ultimate success rate of 209/220 (95.0%). It substantially outperformed baselines including ASPIRE (75.5%), CaP-Agent0 powered by the powerful GPT-6 Astra Pro (60.0%), and RATs (41.8%). Looking at round-by-round progress, success jumped from 28.6% in Round 1 to the high 70s around Rounds 4–5 when prompt revisions (coordinating the perception-action loop) took effect, before reaching 95.0% as cumulative skill bug fixes were integrated in later rounds.

### IV-C Q2: What Drives the Improvement? (Ablation of Diagnostic Inputs)
Ablations removing the Video Analyzer (51.8%), removing the Privileged Agent (50.9%), or removing both (50.9%) all suffered drops of more than 26 percentage points compared to full RPG at Round 5 (78.2%). This shows that effective code revisions require both the "ground-truth reference trajectory" from the privileged agent and the "video-based failure analysis" from the Video Analyzer working in concert.

### IV-D Q3: Does Modifying the Library Alone Provide Value?
When holding the prompt and reasoning model fixed and comparing only before and after skill code modifications, success on targeted tasks rose sharply from 26/40 (65.0%) to 37/40 (92.5%). For instance, in the "lift" skill, a bug that treated actions as complete when the arm had only risen 4.6–5.1 cm against the commanded target was resolved, boosting lift success from 1/13 to 11/11.

### IV-E Q4: Does It Transfer to Physical Robots?
On three quantitative tasks with the physical YAM robot (putting a ball in a drawer and closing it, folding a towel, and hand-over of a bowl), RPG achieved a perfect 30/30 (100%) success across 10 trials per task. In comparison, CaP-Agent0 with GPT-6 Astra Pro achieved only 4/10 on the ball task and 1/10 on the bowl hand-over, highlighting RPG's stable execution on multi-stage complex tasks. Furthermore, RPG succeeded in zero-shot deployment across 5 unseen tasks, including "open scissors" and "uncap a marker."

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: Bottlenecks and Potential in Autonomous Improvement
sections.summary: We demonstrated that robot performance can be dramatically upgraded without touching model parameters, solely through autonomous refactoring of shared skill code and prompts. Managing API parallel limits and skill dependencies remains future work.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated that combining privileged failure diagnosis with cross-task regression testing enables autonomous improvement of robot systems through updates to shared code and prompts alone, without fine-tuning model weights.

The 100% success rate on the physical robot underscores that a high-quality, well-maintained shared skill library provides an exceptionally strong foundation for adapting to physical environments.

On the other hand, the authors note several limitations: API rate limits when running two types of agents across 22 tasks become a bottleneck for improvement speed, and as the number of tasks grows, code dependencies between skills become more tangled, complicating merging. Future work is expected to introduce quota-aware scheduling and dependency-aware integration processes.

captions.F6: Zero-shot qualitative real-world deployments. Five unseen tasks—"open scissors," "uncap marker," "pull tissue," "erase whiteboard," and "unscrew bottle cap"—are executed with zero additional training.

takeaways: Substantial performance gains can be achieved without model weight updates (LoRA or fine-tuning), purely through autonomous revision and debugging of a coded skill library and system prompt.
Failure diagnosis that compares normal agent runs against a privileged agent with ground-truth simulator state via video analysis is exceptionally effective.
Because shared library modifications can easily trigger regressions on other tasks, a cross-task pass/fail verification gate using a fixed evaluation suite is essential.
limitations: As the number of tasks increases, API call volume, cost, and rate limits during parallel execution become bottlenecks in the improvement cycle.
When multiple skill revision candidates arise simultaneously, code dependency conflicts increase the risk of merge failures.
Initial setup still requires human verification when creating and validating simulation environments and success checking functions (check_success).
